Mr. Speaker, I desire to direct the attention of the government, through the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), to the serious fuel situation in Ontario, as set forth in a letter to me from the United Farmers Co-operative Company Limited. This organization, as the minister knows, is working in conjunction with the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and other bodies in an effort to solve the acute coal situation in Ontario. The company object to the fact that only another 25,000 tons of coal is to be moved, and they say:
This in our estimation would be a calamity. There is an emergency throughout Ontario to be met im-


Alberta Coal
mediately on the fuel situation. During the past two weeks we have been in communication by long distance telephone to points throughout all parts of the province, and have made it our business to inquire of our people as to the fuel situation in their district, and we find that coal at almost every point is very scarce.
We find that coal dealers who have been counting on receiving supplies of coke and Pocohontas coal are disappointed in this. Deliveries of this have not come forward as expected. Coke, as we all know, is practically off the market at the present time, and will likely be very scarce until spring. Deliveries of Poco-hontas Coal are slow, and unless an adequate tonnage of Alberta coal is secured for immediate delivery, the situation will create hardship in many localities.
I bring this to the attention of the government in the hope that the minister will be able to assure the House that every possible effort will be made in accordance with the proper procedure to induce the railway companies to consider the hauling of this coal.

Mr. Speaker,
may I point out for the benefit of the House that each province has a fuel commissioner? In the cas9 of Ontario, this official is Mr. Ellis. He is directly in touch, so far as I know, with every district of his province, and is well aware of the local requirements. He has power to direct coal shipments to any point he deems desirable and to take such other measures as he sees fit to relieve any fuel shortage. The federal government is always glad to co-operate in relieving any emergency, but Mr. Ellis and the coal operators of Alberta have been dealing directly with Sir Henry Thornton and his board of management. As my hon. friend is aware, there is no movement of this coal over the Canadian Pacific railway; it is all confined to the Canadian National railways. I want it to be distinctly understood that Sir Henry Thornton announced specifically that he was hauling this coal at seven dollars a ton as an emergency measure. I have no doubt that so long as the emergency exists he will continue to bring in Alberta coal.

Mr. Speaker, when at six o'clock yesterday I moved the adjournment of the debate I was discussing railway construction in the several provinces from 1907 to 1920, and the increased railway mileage then built. During this period the increase in railway mileage constructed in Saskatchewan was 4,200; Ontario, 3,363; Alberta, 3,181; British Columbia, 2,639; Quebec, 1,425; Manitoba, 1,329; New Brunswick, 310; Nova Scotia, 109; Prince Edward Island, 12.
Order. Might I suggest that hon. members should not carry on too many conversations? I have to strain my ears to understand what the hon. gentleman is saying.

These figures, Sir, show
that the percentage increase in railway mileage within each of the provinces for the same period was as follows:
Alberta, 238; Saskatchewan, 208; British Columbia, 155; Ontario, 57; Manitoba, 43; Quebec, 40; New Brunswick, 21; Nova Scotia, 8; Prince Edward Island,

Then consider the amount of Dominion aid given to each of the provinces by way of subsidies, construction of the National Transcontinental railway, the purchase of the Canadian Northern railway, the practical assumption of the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the aid given to the Canadian Pacific Railway. These payments or contributions by provinces are as follows-* and I am giving the figures in round millions:
Ontario, 288; Quebec, 158; British Columbia, 167; Manitoba, 138; Alberta, 128; Saskatchewan, 163; New Brunswick, 28; Nova Scotia, 21; Prince Edward
Island, 8.
For canal construction and enlargement from 1867 to 1925, the capital expenditure in round figures was 225 millions, of which about 20 millions was spent prior to confederation
The Address-Mr. Cantley

To the balance of, say, 200 millions, expended since 1867, is to be added the estimated approximate cost of completing the Welland ship canal, about 54 millions, and this in addition to about 61 millions already expended! on this new work up to the end of the last fiscal year; or, a grand total since 1867 of 280 millions, when the Welland ship canal work now in progress is completed. Of this great sum about $650,000, or less than three-eighths of one per cent was spent on the half mile St. Peter's canal in Cape Breton.
Now Scotia has nearly twenty per cent of the whole population of Ontario, and more than twenty-five per cent of the rural population of that province, but Ontario received nearly $1,400 for every dollar Nova Scotia received by way of railway expenditure, and up to the clos'e of 1923 more than $150 for every dollar expended in Nova Scotia by the federal government on canals. Nova Scotia in 1920 had twenty-four per cent more population than Alberta, while that province received as milway aid from the Dominion more than six times as much as Nova Scotia. Saskatchewan, with practically the same population got 163 odd millions, against 21 millions for Nova Scotia, or nearly eight times as much. British Columbia fared even better, for while the population of Nova Scotia was twenty per cent greater, she got but slightly over one-eighth as much Dominion railway expenditure. Manitoba received nearly seven times as much as Nova Scotia, and Quebec more than seven times as much. We have not forgotten that a few miles of privately-owned branch lines were taken over in Nova Scotia, and several such railways in New Brunswick, but at much below the cost of construction, and in ail the expenditure did not amount to five per cent of that spent in any one of the western provinces.
The province of Nova Scotia gave in land grants to Nova Scotia railways now comprised in the Canadian National Railways,
160,000	acres. The province's proportion of the lands given in grants to other railways, also now merged in the Canadian National system, aggregate 1,770,000 acres. As a partner in confederation Nova. Scotia bad, and by right still has, a substantial interest in these lands and in the benefit derived from this or other such exploitation, though made chiefly in the prairie provinces for railway development there.
Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba were all allowed to extend their boundaries into the territories abutting on these provinces, and so added immense areas-some of great mineral value-to their respective domains. No such advantages came to Nova Scotia, and no com-

pensation has yet been made to Nova Scotia for those portions of the territory so alienated from the Dominion and given to these other provinces. Nova Scotia's interests as one of the four original partners who acquired and paid for these lands is being ignored. I repeat, Sir, Nova Scotia as one of the original partners in confederation has contributed! in proportion to her population to all the national expenditure of the Dominion, and should have realized a proportionate advantage with the other provinces. Neither in railway mileage, railway expenditure, canal construction, nor the free traffic thereon, has she received back a proportion more than, trifling. No share of the prairie public domain has been given her or any compensation for her proportion given to other provinces.
The cost of transportation on the Intercolonial railway has been- doubled, and in many important oases more than doubled, thus virtually cancelling the only commercial consideration promised at confederation. Our basic products are practically dftty free today, and1 we are left not only without protection, but the canal system, to the building of which we have contributed our share, supplies free transportation not only to Quebec, Ontario and the central western provinces, but also to our foreign competitors, who pushed three million tons of soft coal and a considerable tonnage of iron and steel through these waterways into Canada during the season 1923-4.
These Unfavourable conditions, Mr. Speaker, which make it impossible for Nova Scotia to do any volume of profitable business with her sister provinces west of the ancient city of Quebec, are as depressing as they are powerful in effect. Appreciation of the situation is reflected in the building programme of the Dominion for the past year, which in the Contractors Journal is forecast at eighty million dollars. Of this amount it is said that five-eighiths, or thirty millions, will be spent in Ontario, and but one million in the three Maritime provinces. In other words, it is expected that the Maritimes, with a population of one-fifth of that of Ontario, will thus spend on new construction this year only one-fiftieth of the amount to be spent in Ontario. I ask: Why?
A few days ago before I left home to come to Ottawa I saw eighteen expert artisans leave New Glasgow for the United States. These artisans, some of the best mechanics we have in this country, followed nearly three thousand others, most of them equally expert, who have left either New Glasgow or within a radius of five miles of that town within the last two years. Why did they leave? Why were we not able to provide employment in

The Address-Mr. Cantley
this country for those skilled artisans? Why is it necessary for them to leave the Maritime provinces and go to Detroit, Boston, and other points in the United States to get employment? Mr. Speaker, we used to talk some years ago, and I have heard a good deal of that talk myself sitting in the gallery here in past years, about remittance men, but I want to tell the House that we have to-day a large number of remittance men, not in Canada, but in the United States- Canadians who have been forced to go over there, and who, after paying for their board and living expenses, are remitting from week to week and month to month what they can save to maintain their families in Nova Scotia and the other Maritime provinces.
Any serious attempt to investigate the two questions to which I have referred will bring to light the realization of a deep-seated and widespread situation where, due to unfair territorial treatment, tariff inequalities and disappointing traffic conditions, the natural development of the Maritime resources is restricted and the opportunities for employment similarly affected.
I have made little or no reference to the question of protection for our Maritime industries. During each of the months of June and July last there was imported into this country from the United States about
55,000	tons of steel; I do not know what the total tonnage imported in August, September and October was, but for the month of November last we imported into this country from the United States 68,000 tons of steel, seven-eighths of which could have been produced equally well in Canada. Only a few days before I left home, I was in Stellarton, three miles distant from the town of New Glasgow where I live, and there the Public Works department are building a post office. In the construction of that building some structural steel is being used, and what did I find? I looked at the steel and I found rolled into it the name of the Carnegie Steel Company of the United States. The same material could have been bought and was in store at the works at New Glasgow, within four miles of where that building was being erected. There was in store at the works at New Glasgow 6,000 tons of it, 560 different sections of various shapes and sizes, all available for that work. Why was that not used? Why do we bring in, why are we allowed to bring in, American material for use in the construction of public buildings when within four miles of that construction there is ample material available for the purpose, when Canadian steel is stored and
remains uncalled for and unsold so near that construction? That is a condition of affairs, Mr. Speaker, which is not creditable to this country, and it is a condition of affairs that bears hardly upon the province from which I come. During recent years between
600,000	and 700,000 tons of foreign steel has annually come into the Dominion of Canada, and I repeat, 90' per cent of that steel could have been and should have been manufactured within the Dominion of Canada. I do not intend to delay the House much longer in dealing with this phase, but I expect to refer to this question of protection for our iron and steel and coal industries at some later date.
Would the hon. member tell us what is the difference between the American price and the Canadian price for that structural steel? Could it be bought cheaper in the United States?

In reply to the hon.
member, I am not selling steel for the Carnegie Steel Company, and I do not know what their price was.
Hon. gentlemen opposite, the S.O.S. voiceless operators of the derelict government, of which nearly half the officers and fully half the crew are missing, but who, for the time being, are the trustees of the people of this country, the owners of the Canadian National railway system, and as such trustees appoint the board of directors, the president and general manager of that road. They are the masters of the men whom they have appointed, just as the shareholders of any corporation are the masters of the board of directors, the general manager and the other executive officers of that concern. These same trustees for the people of Canada, the owners of the road, did during the last week refuse to the coal miners of Nova Scotia, and of Cape Breton particularly, railway rates on the product of their labour. The rate asked for was in no wise more onerous to the railway than the rate accorded on the movement of coal from Alberta to Ontario. The rate asked for was on a much higher per ton basis than that at which food products are carried from Montreal to Atlantic ports for export overseas, which food products are worth many times the value per ton of coal. I do not care who is going to pay the difference in freight; that is not the point. The point is this:	The railway carried coal for the
western province of Alberta last year, and we ask, we demand, the same consideration in regard to a much smaller quantity of our coal at the present time. Hundreds of miners are to-day idle at Sydney Mines. They
The Address-Mr. Cantley

could be put to work, and would be put to work, if we were given the same advantage in the matter of the movement of a small tonnage of coal as has been accorded our western friends. As I have already said, I have no objection whatever to the movement of that coal from Alberta. I am very glad it has been moved, and so far as I can judge, the railway has not shown or made any attempt to show that a loss was incurred on the movement of that coal.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) gave some of us on this side of the House a couple of weeks or more ago what we understood to be a distinct assurance, indeed a definite promise, that the rate of $3.25, which we had asked on that small movement of coal from Sydney Mines to Montreal, would be put in force, and at once. That was not done although day by day from before the closing of the House on Monday evening, January 25, until Friday of last week, the Minister of the Interior on repeated occasions intimated that he would arrange the matter "to-morrow." Mr. Speaker, the greatest minister who ever held the portfolio of Minister of the Interior in this country was at one time referred to by the Indians of the Northwest as "Old To-morrow." Had they known the present Minister of the Interior, who I am sorry is not in his seat, had they had the experience which we have had with him in the last couple of weeks, would have dubbed him "Big Old Day After To-morrow." May I tell him and the other ministers opposite that the members from Nova Scotia will continue this agitation until the rate is granted and justice is done in this matter. It may be in the memory of some of the older members of this House that a great many years ago the late Hon. Peter Mitchell, the man who as minister organized the Department of Marine and Fisheries at the inauguration of confederation in 1867, for several successive years brought up in this House the question of justice to widow O'Leary, whose cow had been killed on the Intercolonial in 1878. For five years he continued to press the claims of widow O'Leary, and he kept the House in their seats one whole night until eight o'clock next morning when finally he obtained $40 as remuneration for the cow that had been [DOT] killed five years before. I want to tell the minister and hon. gentlemen opposite that so far as we on this side of the House are concerned, we have determined to follow the Hon. Mr. Mitchell's course, and all the resources open to hon. members of this House will be availed

of to the end that justice shall be done us in this matter of coal rates.
The railway construction from the Pacific to the Atlantic determined on in Canada in 1904 has cost practically two thousand millions of dollars. Of this great sum the Maritime provinces have contributed, or equally with the other provinces borne the burden of, one-tenth or more. Hansard supplies evidence that when parliament authorized and ordered this vast railway project, definite promises were made by prominent ministers of the crown that the carrying trade of the Dominion should pass east and west and through Canadian ports, and not south through or to United States ports. As to that there can be no dispute, and in the absence of such envisaged traffic for our St. Lawrence-Maritime ports the project of 1904 could not and would not have been carried through parliament. True there were doubters as to this result, and opposition to the project. Hon. A. G. Blair, then a cabinet minister for New Brunswick, asserted that the outcome would be disappointing to the Maritime ports and people, inasmuch as Canadian freight would be diverted to Portland and other American ports. Was he right? Why did he leave the government? Why did he quarrel with his chief? Because he was convinced that the construction of that road would be followed by the very condition which prevails to-day. I fancy, Mr. Speaker, that every member of the House has seen day after day, during several past wTeeks, statements as to the volume of trade passing through Fort William and Port Arthur en route for Europe and I shall not now tire the House with quoting those tonnage figures though under my hand. During November last, Great Britain bought 24,095,814 bushels of Canadian grain. Of this quantity 18,610,104 bushels went via United States ports, and only 5,845,710 bushels through Canadian ports. During the four months, August to November last, 63,632,830 bushels of our wheat went out through United States ports and but 17,144,207 bushels through Canadian ports. The great bulk of Canadian grain exported was carried by United States railways, and shipped through United 'States ports, to their great profit and our corresponding loss. Why wns such an enormous expenditure incurred in connection with the Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific railways? Why deprive Canadian railway men and Canadian ocean port workers of the handling of Canadian products shipped abroad? Why continue to build up Portland and starve the Intercolonial railway and our Maritime ports? Why build elevators at Halifax and make no use of them? Why have railway officials


The Address-Mr. Cantley
write as to the pending disposal of the Portland Grand Trunk terminals when an election is in prospect' and progress, and continue to expend money on and route grain through those terminals when the election is over; and now when winter is here suggest that pel haps a beggarly half million bushels may be shipped from Halifax some time, when nearly six millions went through Portland last month? Truly the people of the Mari-times are long suffering and slow to wrath. Such conditions breed disorder, and disaster will follow unless promises made to, and accepted in good faith by the Maritime people are redeemed, and that soon. Canadian products must be carried over Canadian railways and shipped through Canadian ports if Canadian confederation is to continue. Persistence iu the present policy of routing Canadian traffic will destroy the Dominion of Canada and that without very much delay.
As to the royal commission promised in the Speech from the Throne, we have seen many royal commissions appointed by the government of the party opposite. These have settled few if any difficulties. The Maritime provinces have commissioned twenty-four representatives, all natives of those provinces, all acquainted with the difficulties that confront their people, to deal with their interests. They are the commissioners appointed by the people of the Maritimes to speak for them and to inform this honourable House as to the disabilities from which the Maritime provinces suffer. May we suggest to those who now propose a royal commission that we know the smell of red herring, and that scent will not now lead any of us astray.
As to the Intercolonial railway, the leaders of both political parties in Canada publicly stated, during the election campaign of 1921, that they would restore the control and management of the Intercolonial railway to Moncton, with the further understanding that the road would be maintained and operated in the interests of the Maritimes and under the direction of Maritime officials. That promise, Mr. Speaker, must be carried out and the Intercolonial railway separated from the central and western portions of the Canadian National system. In that Intercolonial system must be included the Prince Edward Island railway and all the lines and mileage between Sydney, Halifax, St. John and the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, and access must be given to and adequate terminal facilities provided at Montreal. The Intercolonial as thus defined must be operated and managed from Moncton at traffic rates and with facilities such as will make possible trade between the Maritime provinces and 14011-57
the other provinces of the Dominion. That is my demand so far as the Intercolonial railway is concerned, and to that demand I intend to adhere while I am in this House.
May I, Sir, thank you for your patient courtesy and also the House for the considerate hearing accorded me. Two sentences will suffice to express all I now wish to add. We are asked, and have been asked repeatedly, "What do the Maritimes want?" Well, we have informed the House of some of our disabilities; we have referred to the conditions of the union as expressed and understood by our people prior to 1867-conditions and understandings not implemented. We have called your attention to the causes of [DOT]our dissatisfaction. May not we of the eastern provinces, cajoled into union, suggest, and that without any wish to appear sarcastic, that those sections of the Dominion whose cities have grown in population, wealth and influence, who are the chief beneficiaries of confederation, and who sometimes reproach the Maritimes with being slow and unprogressive, that they should propose and provide a practical and effective remedy for the ills of the Maritime provinces? We wait their reply, and on that answer our future action as members of the confederation will depend.

I
feel somewhat handicapped, in fact very much handicapped, in having to address the House from this seat, because I am aware that whatever poor simple rustic remarks I may make will be over-shadowed, and always will be, by the eloquence, the ability and the diction of my deskmate the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). It is appropriate that we should sit together, having both been elected on an independent ticket, and in some respects our ideas are in accord. In others they are distinctly not but I think we can agree to differ, and I hope we will learn from each other by our proximity. I hope the hon. member for Labelle will give me an opportunity of learning something of the charm, the beauty and the gracefulness of his native language, while I on my part will endeavour, at least by ocular demonstration, to impress upon him the benefit of an upbringing consisting mostly of porridge and the shorter catechism, both sound material for body and mind.
Of the various motions and anti-motions, amendments and sub-amendments which have come before the House during the last month or so, which have engaged our attention and for the most part wasted our time, there was none on which I thought it was necessary for me to speak, as coming from British Colum-

The Address-Mr. Neill

bia, or the district I represent, until we came to the amendment now more particularly under consideration. With regard to the earlier motions, I think they can be disposed of more easily. Many of the arguments upon which they were based have -been more or less tacitly, in some cases actually, admitted to be unsound by hon. members opposite. For instance, take the argument advanced that this government had no right to call parliament together. It has been admitted by members on the opposite side of the House that they had an absolute right to call parliament. Precedent all the way down the line shows that if they had only been successful in winning ten seats they still had a right to call parliament and be defeated in the House. All that could be asked, was a speedy calling of the House. That argument is no longer advanced, even by those who made use of it perhaps for partisan purposes.
Then again the question of the matter of plurality of votes has been much dealt with. That is that the Conservative party had gained a majority of the total votes in Canada. Even if that were so-and it is a debatable subject, because on account of having three parties in the field it is always possible for the two parties to combat the suggestion that the other party had a plurality-but even if that were so, it again is an utterly untenable argument that for that reason they were entitled to form the government, because we have only to look at British history, and I think possibly at Canadian history, to see where the government has been carried on successfully with a substantial majority in the House, when it did not possess a plurality of the votes of the country. Again, if that argument is tenable- and hon. members opposite advanced it at great length and very frequently-why are they not willing to extend its application to an individual member; that is to say, that a man shall not represent less than fifty per cent of his electors in the House. But they have gone on record solidly against the transferable vote I do not know the exact position in this House, because we have not the full details, but we know that in the last House there was a considerable number of members who did not represent fifty per cent of their electors, and yet the argument was never used against them that they had not obtained a plurality of votes in their constituencies. It is well known to any student of British and Canadian history that neither the King of England nor the Governor General in Canada has recognized anything but majorities in parliament. Eurther than 
that, he has no right to go below the surface, to question that majority, or to pay any attention to what that majority consists of, whether it is one, solid, united party or made up of half a dozen parties.
A good deal of argument was advanced along that line, and we went back as far, I think, as the reign of Queen Elizabeth to get precedents, which is a long time to go back for precedents. I am surprised no hon. member on either side of the House presented a precedent that occurred in Canadian history not very long ago, and with the permission of the House I will mention it. Some twenty-five years ago in British Columbia a similar condition existed in the local legislature. The government had got down to a majority of one, and by and by one member on the government side turned his vote and the government were defeated. There were only two parties. That happened one afternoon, somewhere about this hour of the day. During the evening negotiations took place, and next morning the premier went to the lieutenant governor, and assured him that he was now in a position to say that he had a majority behind him to carry on the business of the country. The lieutenant governor refused to accept his assurance and insisted on his resignation. He did not resign at the moment, but went back to the House which sat that afternoon, and a resolution of confidence in the government of the day was passed by a -majority of either eight or nine, which was a substantial majority in a house of that size. The members voted confidence in the government as then constituted, and I wish to -point out that this majority was not obtained by the adherence of members of a third group, but it was obtained from the opposite side of the House. They arranged to support the government. The premier went back fortified with this resolution of the House and told the lieutenant governor he was now not only able to obtain the support of the House, but he had been supported by a vote of confidence of eight or nine, whereas he had only been defeated by one vote the day before. The lieutenant governor refused to accept that assurance and insisted on his resignation. The lieutenant governor then sent for another member of the House, who eou-ld not command a majority, and the House was prorogued-not dissolved-without having carried on the business of the country. Naturally representations were made to Ottawa and the lieutenant governor was advised that his action was unconstitutional, and that he should have accepted the advice of his minis-

The Address-Mr. Neill
ter when he said he had a sufficient majority to carry on and should pay no attention to suggestions as to how he had obtained that majority. He was further advised that, in view of the circumstances, he should insist that the member whom he had called on to form a government should either call parliament together again or immediately have a general election. The lieutenant governor was so advised but he did not compel the new premier to do either. The premier went on under what was practically a dictatorship of the country for four or five months. Then an election was held and his party was snowed under. He came back with five or so of a following. In view of those circumstances, the lieutenant governor was asked for his resignation. It was held that he had acted unconstitutionally, and when his attention was called to it he had paid no attention.
I might mention the lieutenant-governor of the province and the government at Ottawa were of the same political persuasion, so it was not a case of party politics. I think that is abundant proof that a premier who can command a majority of the House, as the present government is able to do, is entitled to go on without reference to the other questions as to whether he should or should not have resigned before parliament met, and so on. So much for the constitutional amendments which have taken up so much of our time and which, I submit, were more or less for party advantage. Of course, I do not object to that, because that is the right of hon. members, but the time has come when we should take it as read and go on with the business of the country.
We come next to the amendment which reads:
We desire respectfully to express regret that the Speech from the Throne gives no indication of policy designed to enlarge the volume of employment in Canada. And so on-
Perhaps I am wrong; I am only expressing my opinion; but to my mind that is clearly intended to do what is known as catching the labour vote in this House. That is to say, the labour members are supposed to vote in favour of it because it is an appeal along the line of employment. It has the same appeal to me, whatever value it possesses, because, although I was not elected directly as a labour member, the same as my hon. friends to my right, I got the support very largely, indeed almost entirely of labour in the last contest, and I propose to give labour such support as I can in this House in return, not solely to support class labour legislation, because I was not so elected, but to give labour my 14011-57J	.
support, in recognition of the fact that labour has as much right to representation in this House as any other class; that, numerically, it is very poorly represented, and that it has some rights which have been due to it for some time past. Therefore, the merits of that appeal as regards employment would arouse my sympathy as well as that of my hon. friends to my right. Somebody said: Surely in vain is the net spread in sight of the bird. History tells us that it can be spread again and again in sight of the bird, and the bird or the sucker, as the case may be, does bite a certain percentage of times but not always.
I do not, however, think the percentage of suckers in this House is any greater than it is in the country at large. In this case the-trap is a vote of want of confidence against the government. That is carefully concealed! by the bait spread like a thin sheet of white paper on top of the snow. We are told that-by voting for this amendment we shall further the cause of employment in Canada. It is unfortunate that the present position of this House is such that one cannot give what one might call a sympathetic vote in a matter of this kind without following it through to the ultimate result. In this case, it means that anyone who votes in the spirit of sympathy with the idea so expressed, has to vote for want of confidence in and to defeat the government. It is unfortunate that that condition exists, but it doe3 exist. As to the assertion that the Speech from the Throne does not make any provision in regard to employment, the language of the amendment is this:
No indication of policy designed to enlarge the volume of employment in Canada, etc.
There are in the Speech from the Throne several things which, I think, could be held as producing employment, but I will quote only one sentence and it is this:
My government propose to submit provisions for the completion forthwith of the Hudson Bay railway.
If that does not suggest an immediate and large volume of employment, I do not know what it means. Incidentally, I do not agree with the building of that'railway, but that is beside the point. A proposition calling for an expenditure of from $3,000,000, according to the brightest optimists, to $50,000,000, according to the more sombre ones, must largely promote employment in this country. Therefore, I would suggest that the amendment is hardly applicable in strict terms to the Speech from the Throne in that regard at least.
To those in my constituency and in British Columbia generally who wish employment in the way of requiring it or those, such as trades-

men and producers who, so to speak, live by the workers' business, it is of far greater importance that such questions should be settled as old age pensions, suitable restrictions for Japanese immigration and questions connected with changes in the criminal code and some other matters, than as to who should govern Canada. I do not know about other parts of Canada, but in British Columbia we are getting rapidly into a condition of almost apathy as to who does govern Canada. We only look to see what legislation will be enacted by either party, and the question of which party is in power is indifferent to us provided that legislation is enacted for the benefit of the people. As regards the measures which I have mentioned, we have a distinct statement by the government that legislation along these lines will be introduced at this session. I have to ask myself this question-and I would almos*' leave it to the fair-mindedness of the right hon. gentleman himself: Was I not right, on that occasion at least, in supporting the government, in grasping the substance rather than accepting the shadowy hope held out by my right hon. friend opposite? Another point which is of vital importance to us in that regard is this. When the government says, "We will do this and so," we have a very reasonable belief they will carry it out because, if they do not, they may lose support. But if we accept merely the assurances of hon. gentlemen opposite and they come into power, we have no assurance that they will carry out even any pledges they make, because they can always appeal to the country. That is n point of view which must appeal to men anxious for certain specific legislation.
In Comox-Alberni and indeed in British Columbia generally,, the employment situation, while not as good as we would like to have it-it very seldom is-is not as bad as it might be and as it was for years past. These are the government returns issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce and, as far as I know, they are correct. They have been carried on since 1920 and they began taking 100 as a basis for the people who were employed in the various industries on the first of January, 1920. In September, 1925, the index figure for British Columbia was 114.2,

the largest ever since these returns were commenced and larger than the figure for any other province of the Dominion. That is an increase of 14.2 per cent over the figure for 1920. I am naturally speaking about British Columbia only. At the end of December last, while conditions were not so favourable, because, as the House knows, British Columbia is a country largely of seasonal employment and in the winter time many operations like canneries shut down, but even with that handicap the index stood at 100.5 or higher than it had been for December 31 since 1920. That shows that employment is certainly not getting worse in British Columbia and in the district that I represent.
Speaking more particularly now for the district of Comox-Alberni. I may say that much of this enhanced employment is 4 p.m. due to two causes, one being the Australian treaty and the other the reduction of duty put through by the government at the last session on sawmill machinery. This reduction in duty encouraged the establishment of sawmills in British Columbia and more particularly in my constituency, whereas before the people used simply to export the logs.
During the election an army, I might call it, because their numbers were almost as the sands of the sea, of election workers pobred into Comox-Alberni, and as they swept through the district like a horde of hungry locusts, not seeking whom they might devour, but devouring everything they could, one of their contentions was: Look at the exportation of our bright young blood to the United States 1 They said, " Look how we have been depopulated" and they rang the changes on that in every possible direction. Well the only answer I could make was to ask them this simple question, "Are they taking their houses with them?" I noticed years ago in this town and that, that there were streets of empty houses and to-day they are all filled up. If therefore, the people are going away they must be taking their houses with them, and that is an argument they could not very well meet. They then said, " Oh, but it is not the married people who are going, but the younger ones, the future generation, our boys and girls." Well, in answer to that I suggested that they look at the election lists. Where there were 19 names on the list at one polling station in 1921, there are now one hundred and thirty-four voters who actually cast their ballots in the last election. Now we come to the motion for the adjournment of the House for six weeks. I am afraid that I must regard the opposition to, and amendment to this motion also as designed, if not for obstructive purposes at least for party advantage, although there is no particular objection to the latter. The suggestion has been made again and again in support of the contention that the House should not adjourn that this country is in a horrible condition for want of legislation and that it is imperative that the House should proceed to pass that legislation. Before I deal with the amount of legislation which wie are likely to put through in this House if we continue at the rate we are going at present, I want to point out that in 1922 the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne was not passed until March 23, a week later than we should meet on the present occasion if we took the proposed adjournment. And in 1924 the Address was adopted on Mlarch 18, three days later than parliament would reassenible after this adjournment. In 1925 'the Address was passed earlier having been adopted on February 12. The fact is however, that on the average we should not be behindhand in the business of the House if we adjourned now after passing the Address in Reply and proceeded with legislation after coming back on March 15.
It has been suggested that in the event of no' adjournment we might spend a great deal of time making stump speeches. I think the leader of the opposition (M|r. Meighen) refuted that idea and said that we had a perfect, right to speak in this House with a view to influencing the Voters in any particular district in which a by-election was being 'held. That is perfectly true on the face of it; that is our right. Burt there is hardly ever a right which is so closely safeguarded that it could not be abused, and in this case abuse would inevitably follow. Instead of making speeches intended to further legislation in parliament for the benefit of the country we would infallibly on both sides of the House engage in campaign speeches in the hope of swaying the electors in the particular constituency in which a by-election happened to be imminent at the moment.
I hope the House will excuse me for returning to British Columbia by way of illustration, but I do not know of any better province to which I could refer for this or any other purpose, and in this connection I would point out that the same condition obtained once out there. The government had a small majority and there was a by-election pending that might have upset it. It was proposed by the government that the House should take an adjournment of two weeks and I, as a supporter of the administration of the time, opposed the idea. I was of the opinion that if we adjourned we should lose all that time and the view of those who opposed the adjournment prevailed. We did not adjourn and I regretted the fact afterwards for we sat for two weeks during which time we did not pass one iota of useful legislation nor did we contribute in any constructive way to the public business at all. We simply made stump speeches for the benefit of the electors in the by-election and this demonstrated quite clearly to my mind that it would have been better had we taken the adjournment. There i3 another aspect of the question that suggests itself to me and which, I think, has not been so far touched upon. Suppose that the government had been defeated upon the motion for the adjournment by the opposition. The cry was that the country was impatient for legislation and that parliament should proceed with the public business. Well, as I say, suppose the government had been defeated upon that occasion. Would it not have been absolutely necessary for the leader

of the opposition in all decency to demand and receive an adjournment of at least six or eight weeks in order to enable him to form his government? A good government.

We now come to the amendment moved by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) wherein he expresses regret at the operation of the Australian treaty. The amendment evidently is aimed primarily if not entirely at that treaty in its relation to the dairy industry of Canada and particularly of butter. The vote so far as this amendment is concerned has occasioned more doubt in my mind than any of the previous amendments, not because of any consideration as to the respective virtues of one party or the other but because of the fact that there are conflicting interests affected in the district I represent. The suggestion has been made time and again that the competition of butter sent from Australia would hurt our dairy producers in this country and that means particularly so far as I am concerned, the dairy pioducers of British Columbia. Now I ask myself in this connection three important questions: (1) Will that competition hurt the dairy producers in my district as well as in the province of British Columbia generally- because I must necessarily consider more than the interests of my own constituency alone; (2) Will the injury if there is any injury as a result of the operation of the treaty, be .offset by the advantages which it is admitted 'will accrue, are accruing and have already accrued to the fishing, the lumber and the pulp industries of British Columbia and of any district particularly. There are other advantages that would enure >to eastern Canada in the way of the manufacturing of cars and goloshes, and corsets and so on, but I am not particularly concerned with that at the moment. And (3) Will there be any indirect

benefits to the dairying industry which will offset any losses that may ensue? The indirect [DOT] benefits, it has been suggested, might be larger and better local home markets.
Let me deal in the first place with the actual competition as it exists. I want to set right a misapprehension that seems to be in the minds of some hon. members, and which was obscurely hinted at on one occasion that the Australian government was subsidizing Australian butter to enable that product to compete in our markets. The fact is not so. The reference is to what is called the Pattersen scheme-and this is not associated with the government. This scheme is purely voluntary, not being supported by the government. It depends for its success upon every creamery in Australia joining on a voluntary basis, much as in the case of the wheat pool, the plan being to levy two cents per pound on all butter manufactured and out of this to give a bounty of six cents per pound on the one-third of the total production which is estimated will be exported. It is claimed that this would have the effect of increasing the price of the product consumed at home to the extent of four cents per pound. The scheme is not yet in operation and there is considerable doubt whether it can be carried out. It would not make it easier to ship Australian butter into Canada because the bounty would be paid on all butter exported, not only to Canada but elsewhere as well, and Australian butter will not come here when the seller can get more money for it in the world market.
Something has been said about a strike which occurred in Australia and New Zealand. I will not be positive about this because I have no personal, precise knowledge of the dates. We do know that a strike occurred among the seamen of Australia and New Zealand and it tied up the export of butter in the ordinary way to Great Britain. That helped to create a temporary demand for our butter in Great Britain and we sold considerable quantities there at the time. As soon as the strike was settled, naturally this butter that was kept in cold storage where it'did not improve was immediately rushed to the markets of the Old Country, and that fact accounts for the large quantity of Australian butter that hag been brought here recently. That would not prevail under ordinary conditions. The cost of transporting butter from Australia to Liverpool is substantially the same as from Australia to Vancouver, and if that is correct or nearly correct the tendency must be to ship not to British Columbia but direct by all water route to Liverpool. We

The Address-Mr. Neill
all know that a world commodity must be governed in the matter of price by the rate fixed in the world's markets and which in turn fixes the price that will prevail in any particular locality. My attention has recently been called to an announcement that a large shipment of butter from Australia or New Zealand had been consigned by British purchasers to New York and that on its arrival there, although there is a heavier duty in the United States than we have, it was discovered that it would be more profitable to ship a certain portion of it to the Old Country, keeping a part of the shipment in the United States, and to ship a large proportion to Canada. In this case we should suffer from a very unfair competition inasmuch as the British dealers would use this country as a dumping ground. They could ship the butter from Australia or New Zealand to New York and then it could be diverted wherever it would be most profitable to be disposed of. This is the contention. But there is no danger to be anticipated in that regard because the wording of the Australian act, section 5, I think it is, provides that the product must be consigned on a through bill of lading. I do not know whether this is the exact phraseology of the act, but I do know that it is necessary that the product should be shipped direct. Shipping goods from New Zealand via New York on a direct bill of lading to Montreal would be all right, but when the article is shipped to New York and is there diverted into separate sections it does not come under the Australian treaty and therefore pays the old duty. So that this particular matter is of no great consequence to us.

- look good to me; they have the appearance of super-gods, with the exception of one member who, I might say, looks to me like a beautiful young goddess. That hon. gentleman, endeavoured in a manner hardly compatible with the description I have given of him, to stampede the Progressives by the [DOT] suggestion that anyone who had voted last year for the Australian treaty came back to this House no more. Well, it would be equally tenable for him to say that he had found, as no doubt he could find, that people with names beginning with certain initials had been more unlucky than others in coming back to the House. The fact is that there is nothing at all in the suggestion; it has nothing to do with the Australian treaty and
the hon. member's figures were not right even when handled as they were. He said that no member of the Progressive party who had voted for the treaty had been returned. That is not correct. One out of five came back, not a large proportion it is true, but we must remember that quite a number of the Progressives were left at home in any case. Am I to assume that there is something ominous in having been associated with old age pensions in the past and that anyone who had anything to do with that subject would necessarily be extinguished? Naturally a discussion of butter leads up to the subject of oleomargarine. Members of the last parliament will remember that I took a decided stand in that matter. I wanted to protect the dairy farmer as well as the workingman against the sale of oleomargarine because I considered it just as bad to buy the stuff as to compete against it. I wanted to protect the working people against this injurious product, as well as the farmer, and where did I get support on that occasion? If I remember rightly seven members of the Conservative party voted against the introduction of oleomargarine and fifteen for it. So that only seven members of the Conservative party supported me on that occasion in trying to protect the farmer and the workingman. So I am glad to find that there are now some hon. members opposite who are showing a healthier interest in the welfare of the farmer.

In the redistribution three were cut off from my constituency and two were

Of late years, and of late months particularly, it has become the recognized 
system for this creamery association to spread out. They handle practically all farm products, ice cream even, strawberries, potatoes, lamb, and mutton, and the market for all these products is confined almost entirely to Powell River, because it is close at hand, with only a short haul, and best of all, a home market. In addition, a number of saw mills have sprung up in the district I represent, a number of small ones, and also some large. I could point to at least four large ones which employ a large number of men. They will furnish a market for the neighbouring farm districts, not only for butter, but beef, potatoes, and so on.

When the Meighen government left office in 1921 the amalgamation of the various lines of railway now going to make up what is known as the Canadian National railway system had not been completed. During the election campaign of 1921 the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), then Prime Minister, in a speech delivered in Moncton, gave considerable attention to the railway problem. He stated in the clearest terms the policy of his government and the policy of the board of management as then constituted. That policy was that on completion of the amalgamation the Canadian National railways should be composed of three grand divisions, one for the east, to be managed from Moncton, and the other two to be known as the central and western divisions. The eastern division, the present leader of the opposition said, should comprise the Intercolonial railway and all that part of the Grand Trunk system east of Montreal. Supporters of the Liberal party, as led by Mr. King, sought in every way to discredit my right hon. leader's policy as applied to the eastern division. They said that the Intercolonial railway should be divorced from the Canadian National system, and managed from Moncton, entirely free from outside dictation. They declared this would be done if the Liberal party, led by Mr. King was returned to power, and that the few officials sent to Toronto would be returned to Moncton. Moncton would then be the Chicago of the east. When Mr. King became Prime Minister the old board of management, with Mr. Hanna at the head, was dismissed, and a new board created with Sir Henry Thornton as president. I should like to tell the Minister of the Interior about several other factories in my riding that have been undermined and have had to close their doors since this government came into office. The men interested in those factories are looking forward to the day when a Conservative government will take office and give reasonable protection to those industries. We had a wagon factory established in our town over twenty years ago. It employed two hundred hands, supporting two hundred homes in Petrolia, and they and their dependents helped to consume the products that make a home market for the farmer. What happened? In July 1920, the Petrolia Wagon Works was taken over by the Adams Wagon Works of Brantford, owned and controlled by the Cockshutt Plow Company. At that time Mr. Cockshutt -now Lieutenant Governor of Ontario- stated:
I want to see men working in every corner of your factory. You cannot produce too much. We can sell * more than you can make for the next five years.
What happened? Premier King promised the Progressives that if elected to office he would take the duty off all instruments of production used by the farmers. This immediately created a want of confidence not only among manufacturers but also among the farmers, or the buying public of these products, and business slumped until it was known what King would do. The budget was brought down, and the protection on farm wagons and sleighs was reduced from 17J per cent to 10 per cent. Immediately wagons and sleighs from the south began to come into the we3t largely through catalogue or mail order houses, at prices about on a par with our costs. Those catalogue houses have no warehouses, carry no repair parts, have no selling organization-nothing but cut rate prices, here today, gone tomorrow.

The last few years we have witnessed a very gratifying progress in the dairy industry in Canada, especially in the prairie provinces where the establishment of agricultural industries other than wheat growing is a generally recognized necessity. In 1925 the daily industry returned the largest revenue in its history. Dairy cattle made strong prices at public sales, and the prices for butter and cheese were excellent. The increased output of daily products has been most marked as regards creamery butter, the quantity of which for all Canada has grown from 152,501,900 pounds in 1920 to 278,074,849 pounds in 1924, an increase of about 80 per cent. Factory cheese has remained more nearly stationary, the production having increased during the four years 1920 to 1924 by only 506,674 pounds or from 149,201,856 pounds to 149,707,530 pounds. In the three prairie provinces the production of creamery butter has increased from 34,877,815 pounds in 1920 to 48,515,672 pounds in 1924, an increase of 13,637,857 pounds, or 38 per cent.
Another indication of progress is the increase in the exports of butter. Thus for the calendar year ended December 31, 1921, exports of butter from Canada amounted to 9,132,926 pounds, whilst in 1924 they were 22,343,939 pounds. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1925, they were 24j501,981 pounds as against 13,648,968 pounds in 1924. And exports of butter are now being made successfully from the prairie provinces to the United Kingdom, the United States, the Wesit Indies and to oriental and other countries. That western Canada is building up a reputation for excellence of quality in dairy products is shown by the fact that in the colonial sedtion of the London Dairy Show last October, Alberta butter gained the first prize and gold medal. At this show Canada Won four out of the six prizes offered for Empire-wide competition and western Canada won four out of the six. There are very gratifying indications of progress in dairying, ivhich possesses great possibilities of future development. in western Canada.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is no need for this treaty under these conditions. Let us develop the dairy industry in western Canada and in eastern Canada as well. Let us stand true to that industry and let us see to it that proper legislation is brought down and put through in the interest of that great industry. As a citizen of this Dominion- and I am proud to be one-I shall be only too glad to support any measure, let it be for the expenditure of money or otherwise, that will have for its aim the development not

only of the dairy industry but of the whole of the agricultural industry of this Dominion.

This discussion, it seems to me, has brought out several differences of opinions as to jusf what was the issue in the recent campaign. I should like to preface a few remarks with the very emphatic statement that in West Kootenay the issue was protection, and the people there voiced, with no uncertainty, their absolute lack of confidence in the King government. They were not in accord with the mixed variety of protection suggested by the Prime Minister in the different parts of Canada in which he happened to -be speaking. But they were in accord with the National Policy of protection as declared for by the leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Meighen)-protection for industry, fur the wage earners, for the consumer and for the farmer. They declared emphatically for protection, the basic principle of which was the creation of Canadian payrolls, and protection which reserves to the Canadian farmer the benefits of his home market.
The campaign which returned a Conservative candidate from West Kootenay, British Columbia, was in striking contrast to the utterances and expressed sentiments of the Prime Minister in his opening speech at Richmond Hill when he stressed the statement that he did not want to be hampered, or harassed, or embarrassed, or dictated to, or dominated by a Progressive group, and that unless he had a good working majority of Liberals he would resign. We have not yet had any indications of a resignation. We also had a recent speech of the Prime Minister in Vancouver, just on the eve of the campaign when he said:
The great problems facing Canada cannot be solved by a government without a strong following.
That was no later than last September. So the situation is this, that we have a national problem for the protection of the farmer and this government is not in a position to solve it. The Prime Minister's utterances at Richmond Hill were made on the 5th day of September, and they cannot be accepted as having been made with any degree cf sincerity

because only a few days later the Prime Minister himself appeared in my constituency and there he urged the electors to give their generous support to my opponent who was designated as a Farmer-Labour-Progressive-Independent. I want to refer for just a moment to a matter other than that of agriculture, because it is a fact worthy of note that the Speech from the Throne contains absolutely no reference by way of recognition of the vast natural wealth of British Columbia, the development of which would very largely solve, first of all, the immigration problem, certainly, the unemployment problem, and, lastly, the problem of the exodus of Canadians to the United States. British Columbia has added to the national wealth of this country by its production of coal and coke no less than $260,000,000, and notwithstanding interruptions it yields $10,000,000 per annum. Our fisheries yield $25,000,000, our agriculture, $45,000.000, our industrial revenue, $155,000,000, our forest products, $100,000,000, and our mines $66,000,000. In other words, we add practically $500,000,000 annually to the credit of British Columbia, and this is tending to
build up what is destined to be, not only the greatest city in Canada, but certainly the most important port on the Pacific coast-the city of Vancouver.
Now, I think this discussion also brings out the supposition that the prairie provinces are bearing a very large share of the burdens of Canada to-day-perhaps to them they appear to be more than their share. But I think it would materially advance our national interests, certainly it would enlarge the information of hon. members, regardless of their political affiliations, if they would simply take time between sessions to cover different portions of the Dominion, and I would add- particularly the province of British Columbia. Our chief interests in my district are mining and farming, especially fruit growing. If you come to the historic mining camp of Rossland you could go underground through a concrete shaft for a distance of half a mile and ride in electric cars for thirty miles, and be lost through workings and tunnelings extending over eighty miles, every mile of which has produced one million dollars in wealth. Those eighty million dollars have created a Canadian payroll for three thousand men for the last twenty-five years. And Mr. Speaker, what we need to-day chiefly are Canadian payrolls. You can go down the mountain from our little town six miles and come to the greatest and most modern smelter on the continent, wffiere is produced gold, silver, lead, copper, zinc, antimony and other by-products, 99.99 per cent pure. You can go out to the adjoining district, represented by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. King), and there you will find the richest mine on the North American continent. You can go to the coast and find the Britannia mine, which at one time was considered a white elephant. Its mineral resources are immense. But in the early days science had not advanced to the point where it could make a commercial possibility of that vast body of ore. However, science has since accomplished this. Then, too, you will find the Premier mine, which has paid dividends aggregating $7,000,000 since 1921.
But the point I want to drive home is that while to-day. the mineral development of British Columbia is on the upgrade, and people arc keenly interested in it, yet there is necessary greater action on the part of the government for field and research work. It is the research work, carried on chiefly by private companies, which to-day has resulted in the greatest achievement in metallurgical science. This company did a business of $68,000 last year, and according to this despatch the directors in their annual report called attention to 'The impending peril to the dairy interests of western Canada created by the Australian trade treaty." The despatch further goes on to say that the company will be represented by a delegation of the Western Dairy Association which will shortly wait upon the federal government in this connection. That would be a very interesting interview to attend for those members from Saskatchewan who are favouring this Australian treaty.

There are various other matters which the Speech from the Throne does not mention. I might say a word on a subject which was discussed in the campaign in my district. I think it is a matter for regret that absolutely no mention is made in the Speech from the Throne as to the necessity of looking after the welfare of the returned soldiers. We must

The Address-Mr. Eshng
presume that the government has practically no concern about the returned men. I say that is a national problem. It is one of the problems with which the Prime Minister of this country said he could not deal unless he had a strong following. This government is better informed than anybody else as to the physical condition of the returned men, and particularly the amputation and tubercular cases, and my contention is that this government should see to it that every man in either of those classes is given the opportunity to work. The returned men are not asking for any more than they asked for before they gave their services to this country. They were able to make a living then, and all they ask is an opportunity to make it now. The hon, member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) read an advertisment the other day in which this government guarantees to give immigrants to this country five years' employment. Why, we have returned men in our country who would thank God for five days' employment a month; we have good settlers who have cleared the land and tilled the soil and who would be thankful to get five days' employment a month; and yet we are offering to give newcomers to this country five years' employment. Does not the irony of it strike you, Mr. Speaker?
There is another omission in the Speech from the Throne that is noticeable because it was included in the Prime Minister's manifesto, and that is Senate reform. I had an opponent who was going to abolish the Senate entirely; he was going one better than the Prime Minister. This talk of Senate reform takes us back to the time when Senate reform was a live subject in this House, and the Prime Minister then, to appease all sides, said:	We will have a conference of the
premiers of all the provinces and see what we can do about the Senate. Well, a lot of water has gone over the wheel since that time. At that time there was not one single Conservative premier in the Dominion of Canada, but to-day things are different. There is no use calling a conference of premiers if they are Conservatives, as they are now, and so the Prime Minister has conveniently forgotten about reforming the Senate through a conference of provincial premiers, and now says he will reform it from within. It is remarkable there should be no mention made of Senate reform in the Speech from the Throne. It was a subject that was discussed on every platform in this Dominion, and one would naturally have thought it would be a part of the legislative programme of this government.
There is one other omission in the Speech from the Throne, and I mention it because in my district they were particularly keen to have an old age pension scheme. They feel that people who have come and settled in Canada, tilled the soil and raised their families here should be taken care of in their old age.
I do not believe there is any piece of legislation this government could bring down which would be of so much general importance to the whole of Canada as legislation on old age pensions. It is not a matter of local interest, it is not a matter relating to the Hudson Bay railway or the construction of any other public work or canal which perhaps benefits a particular section. It is a matter of interest to the whole Dominion; yet this government absolutely ignores it and does not even mention it in the Speech from the Throne. It i3 true that according to the concensus of opinion there were attempts-I will not put, it that way, because you have ruled, Mr. Speaker, that references to bribes or purchases are not parliamentary-but I would say that the sympathies of the government were enlisted in this direction perhaps as an expedient for bolding on to power. And so when the acting leader of the government was asked the other day if it was their intention to bring down old age pension legislation, he replied that it was. I should like to ask if .the proposed conference off premiers to deal with the question of old age pensions has taken plaice since last session, because that was the excuse then for not bringing this legislation down.
We have one other matter which interests
the people of Canada to-day and that is the question of taxation. I say, without fear or hesitation that upon this question rests the creation and maintenance of the payrolls of Canada, because those who have .money to invest in the development of our natural resources, and are inclined to do so, are naturally going to stop and inquire what the effect of the present taxation upon their plans is going to be. And so taxation., whether applied to incomes or to industries, has a very important bearing on the development of this country. If by reason of good fortune you happen to have an income of $3,000 a year in Canada you pay a tax of $40. In the United States on the same income you only pay $7.50, a very marked difference. Again, on an income of $5,000 in Canada you pay $120 in taxation as against $37.50 collected on the same amount in the United States. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and gentlemen, iif men with money to invest-the manufacturer or the

Now, just for a moment I want to refer once more to the irony of this provision of five years' employment for new settlers. I want to show you, Sir, that this government since the year 1921 has spent, to be exact, .$10,367,000 on immigration, and I do not believe I am making an extravagant statement when I say they have not one solitary settler to their credit for that very large expenditure-not one.

In other words the government have 35,000 arrivals to their credit for the expenditure of $10,000,000. But actually they do not even have that number, because there is not a member of this House who cannot say that some relative, or some family connection, has not found it impossible to earn a living in Canada and has therefore been obliged to emigrate to the United States. . In conclusion I want to say that the greatest immigration agencj'' any country can ever have is the payroll. It is the Canadian payroll that is going to build up Canada, and when hon. gentlemen opposite try to confuse the issues they are only fooling themselves. You do not see American immigration agents in Canada endeavouring to induce Canadians to locate in the country to the south. Not at all. Their immigration policy, their immigration agent, is the payroll, and it is because the payrolls are there that our young men and women are leaving Canada and going to the United States faster than we can pay them to come to this country. So I say there must be a reduction of taxation which will invite capital to engage in the development of our natural resources, create Canadian payrolls, and bring about- such conditions in this country as will secure, first of all, the return of the five hundred and some odd thousand Canadians who have gone from Canada to the United States. Then you have a basis upon which to start a real immigration policy.
